title: Freelance Bookkeeping Starter Kit
description: Keep your freelance money organised in 30 minutes a month without accounting software: an income and expense ledger with example rows, category guide, monthly close checklist, receipt filing system, tax set-aside planner, 12-week cash flow forecast and a quarterly review with a worked example.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Bookkeeping Starter Kit

A simple, spreadsheet-based way to keep your freelance money organised in about 30 minutes a month. Know what came in, what went out, what you are owed, how much to put aside for tax, and whether next month looks tight, without buying accounting software.

It is built for freelancers and sole traders in their first few years: designers, writers, developers, consultants, tutors, photographers and anyone else invoicing clients directly.

## What's inside

| File | Use it for |
|---|---|
| income-expense-ledger.csv | Your main record: one row per payment in or out, with category, client and receipt reference. Comes with a month of example rows. |
| expense-categories.md | A plain-language list of common categories, what goes in each and what does not. |
| monthly-close-checklist.md | The 30-minute monthly routine that keeps everything up to date. |
| receipt-system.md | How to name, file and keep receipts and invoices so you can find any of them in seconds. |
| tax-set-aside-planner.md | A method for working out a percentage to move into a separate account every time you are paid, with a worked example. |
| cash-flow-forecast.csv | A 12-week look ahead: expected money in, money out, and your balance, so you can spot a tight month early. |
| quarterly-review.md | A one-page review every three months, with a completed example. |

All files open in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or any text editor.

## Quick start (45 minutes, once)

1. **Open a separate bank account** for business money if you can, or at least a separate savings pot for tax. Mixing business and personal money is the single biggest cause of bookkeeping pain.
2. Read **expense-categories.md** and decide on the categories you will use. Fewer is better: 8-12 is plenty for most freelancers.
3. Open **income-expense-ledger.csv**, read the example rows, then delete them and enter this month's payments so far from your bank statement.
4. Read **receipt-system.md** and create the folders it describes.
5. Work through **tax-set-aside-planner.md** to pick your set-aside percentage.
6. Put a recurring 30-minute appointment in your calendar for the first working day of each month, titled "Monthly close".

## Every month (30 minutes)

Follow **monthly-close-checklist.md**. In short: match the ledger to your bank statement, file the receipts, chase unpaid invoices, move money to your tax pot, and update the cash flow forecast.

## Every three months (45 minutes)

Fill in **quarterly-review.md**. It tells you which clients and services earn the most, where money is leaking, and whether your set-aside percentage is still right.

## How the ledger works

Each row is one movement of money:

- **date**: the day it reached or left your bank account (YYYY-MM-DD, so the column sorts correctly)
- **type**: `income`, `expense`, `transfer` (moving money between your own accounts, such as to your tax pot) or `owner` (money you pay yourself or put into the business)
- **category**: from **expense-categories.md** (for income, use the service or product name)
- **description**: what it was, in a few words
- **client_or_supplier**: who paid you or who you paid
- **amount**: always a positive number. The type column says which direction it went
- **invoice_or_receipt_ref**: the file name of the matching invoice or receipt (see **receipt-system.md**)
- **paid_from**: which account (for example `business`, `tax-pot`, `personal-card`)
- **notes**: anything you will want to remember, such as "part business use" or "refund due"

Only `income` and `expense` rows count towards profit. `transfer` and `owner` rows are there so the ledger still matches your bank balance.

In the example month: income 2,250.00, expenses 380.04, so profit is 1,869.96. Another 562.50 went to the tax pot and 1,000.00 was owner pay; neither changes the profit.

## How the cash flow forecast works

Each row is one week of your **business account** (not the tax pot):

```
closing_balance = opening_balance + expected_income - expected_expenses - tax_set_aside - owner_pay
```

Each week's opening balance is the previous week's closing balance. Pick a **safety buffer**, the lowest balance you are comfortable with (many people choose about one month of business costs plus owner pay), and mark `below_buffer` as `yes` for any week that drops under it. When a week passes, replace the estimates with the real numbers and set `actual_or_estimate` to `actual`.

Only put income in the forecast when you are fairly sure of it (an invoice is sent, or a deposit is agreed), and note anything uncertain. The example shows a freelancer who will dip below their buffer in late June unless they act now.

## Notes

This kit is a general record-keeping system, not tax, legal or accounting advice. Tax rules, allowable expenses, deadlines and how long you must keep records all depend on where you live and how your business is set up. Use this kit to stay organised, and check the specifics with your local tax authority or a qualified accountant. A tidy ledger also makes an accountant's time cheaper. The example names and figures are made up for illustration.

This kit pairs well with the Freelancer Get-Paid Kit (invoices and payment reminders) and the Freelance Rate Calculator tool.

files.expense-categories.md:
# Expense Categories

Use a short, consistent list of categories so that at the end of the year you can add up each one in seconds. The list below covers most freelancers. Delete the ones you never use, and only add a new one if something comes up every month.

Whether an expense can be deducted for tax, and how much of it, depends on where you live and on how you use it. This list is for organising your records, not a statement of what is tax deductible. Mark anything you are unsure about in the **notes** column of the ledger and ask your accountant or tax authority.

---

## Common categories

| Category | What goes in it | What usually does not |
|---|---|---|
| **Software and subscriptions** | Design, writing, accounting, project management and cloud storage plans; website hosting; domain names | Personal streaming or entertainment subscriptions |
| **Equipment** | Computers, monitors, cameras, drives, keyboards, headsets, desks and chairs used for work | Items bought mainly for personal or family use |
| **Phone and internet** | Business phone line, mobile plan, home internet | Note the share used for work if it is a mixed personal and business bill |
| **Office and supplies** | Stationery, printer ink, postage, small items under a few tens of currency units | Groceries, household cleaning products |
| **Workspace** | Co-working desk, studio rent, meeting room hire | Your home rent or mortgage (rules on home working costs vary; ask a professional) |
| **Travel** | Train, bus, taxi, parking and mileage for client work or work events | Your normal daily commute, in many countries |
| **Meals and entertainment** | Only if your local rules allow it; keep a note of who and why | Everyday lunches on your own |
| **Marketing** | Website costs not covered above, ads, business cards, portfolio platforms, printed samples | Personal social media spending |
| **Professional services** | Accountant, bookkeeper, lawyer, business adviser, translator | Personal legal matters |
| **Training and books** | Courses, workshops, conference tickets and books that relate to your current work | Training for a completely new career, in many countries |
| **Insurance** | Professional indemnity, public liability, equipment insurance | Personal health or life insurance, unless your local rules say otherwise |
| **Bank and payment fees** | Business account fees, card processing fees, international transfer fees | Fees on your personal account |
| **Subcontractors** | Other freelancers you pay to help on client projects | Your own pay (record that as `owner`, not as an expense) |
| **Cost of goods** | Materials or stock you resell or use to make products you sell | Equipment you keep (put that under Equipment) |

## Income categories

For income rows, use the **service or product** instead of an expense category. This lets you see which kind of work brings in the most money. For example:

- Website design
- Logo design
- Consulting
- Writing
- Workshops and teaching
- Digital product sales
- Retainers

## Rows that are not income or expenses

| Type | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `transfer` | Moving money between your own accounts, such as to your tax pot or savings |
| `owner` | Paying yourself, or putting your own money into the business |

These keep your ledger matching your bank account without making your profit look higher or lower than it is.

## Mixed-use costs

Some costs are partly business and partly personal, such as a phone or home internet. A common approach is:

1. Record the full amount in the ledger.
2. In **notes**, write your best estimate of the work share and how you worked it out (for example "about 50% work: checked one month of call logs").
3. Ask your accountant how to treat it. Keeping your reasoning written down makes that conversation quick.

## Five habits that keep categories clean

1. **Pick the category the day you record the row.** Guessing three months later is where mistakes come from.
2. **Do not create a "Miscellaneous" category.** If more than a few rows a year would go in it, you need a real category.
3. **One category per row.** If a receipt covers two kinds of things, split it into two rows.
4. **Keep refunds in the original category** as a negative note or a separate row marked "refund", so the category total stays accurate.
5. **Review the list once a year.** Merge categories you hardly use.

files.monthly-close-checklist.md:
# Monthly Close Checklist

Do this on the first working day of each month, for the month that just ended. It takes about 30 minutes once you are used to it (the first time may take an hour). Put a recurring appointment in your calendar so it never gets skipped.

Month: ______________   Done on: ______________

---

## 1. Gather (5 minutes)

- [ ] Download last month's statement for every account you use for business: business bank, tax pot, any card that paid a business expense, and any payment provider that pays out to you.
- [ ] Open **income-expense-ledger.csv**.
- [ ] Open your receipts inbox folder (see **receipt-system.md**).

## 2. Match the ledger to the bank (10 minutes)

- [ ] Go through the bank statement line by line. Every line should have a matching row in the ledger. Add any that are missing.
- [ ] Check that each row has a **type**, **category** and **amount**.
- [ ] Look for payments you do not recognise. Investigate each one now, while it is fresh.
- [ ] If a business expense was paid from a personal card, record it with `paid_from` set to that card and a note to repay yourself.
- [ ] Check the closing balance: your ledger's starting balance, plus income, minus expenses, minus transfers out, minus owner pay, should equal the closing balance on your statement. If not, a row is missing or doubled.

## 3. Receipts (5 minutes)

- [ ] Every expense row has a matching receipt or invoice saved and named (see **receipt-system.md**).
- [ ] The file name is in the **invoice_or_receipt_ref** column.
- [ ] Missing receipts: request a copy from the supplier, or write a short note of what it was, when, and why.
- [ ] Receipts inbox is empty: everything filed into the month folder.

## 4. Money you are owed (5 minutes)

- [ ] List every invoice that is sent but not paid, with its due date.
- [ ] Overdue invoices: send the next reminder today.
- [ ] Any work finished last month but not invoiced yet: invoice it today.

| Invoice | Client | Amount | Due date | Days overdue | Next step |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | |
| | | | | | |

## 5. Tax pot (2 minutes)

- [ ] Check that your set-aside percentage was moved to the tax pot for every income row last month (see **tax-set-aside-planner.md**).
- [ ] If any were missed, move the total now and add a `transfer` row.
- [ ] Note the tax pot balance: ______________

## 6. Look ahead (3 minutes)

- [ ] Update **cash-flow-forecast.csv**: replace last week's estimates with the actual figures and add a new week at the end.
- [ ] Look at the lowest balance in the next 12 weeks. If it is below the safety buffer you chose, decide what to do now: chase invoices, delay a purchase or line up more work.
- [ ] Note any large bills coming up (annual software renewals, insurance, tax payments).

## 7. One-line summary

Write one line in your notes or at the bottom of the ledger:

> [Month]: income ______, expenses ______, profit ______, owed to me ______, tax pot ______.

After a few months, these lines show your trend at a glance.

---

## If you fall behind

It happens. Do not try to catch up on six months in one sitting.

1. Start with the **current** month and do a normal close.
2. Then work backwards one month per day until you are caught up.
3. Bank statements are the source of truth. If a receipt is missing for an old expense, record the row anyway with a note, and ask the supplier for a copy.

# Quarterly Review

Every three months, spend 45 minutes stepping back from the day-to-day. Do it right after the monthly close for the last month of the quarter, so your ledger is already up to date.

Fill in the blank version below. A completed example follows it.

---

## Blank review

**Quarter:** ______________   **Done on:** ______________

### 1. The numbers

Add up the ledger rows for the three months (filter by date, then by type). Last quarter's figures come from your previous review.

| | This quarter | Last quarter | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Income | | | |
| Expenses | | | |
| Profit (income minus expenses) | | | |
| Profit as % of income | | | |
| Owner pay taken | | | |
| Tax pot balance at quarter end | | | |
| Money owed to me at quarter end | | | |
| Business account balance at quarter end | | | |

### 2. Where the money came from

| Client or income category | Income this quarter | % of total |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

- Largest single client's share of income: ______ %
- If more than about half of your income comes from one client, write down one step to reduce that risk: ______________________

### 3. Where the money went

| Expense category | This quarter | Last quarter | Worth it? (yes / review / cut) |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |

- Subscriptions I no longer use: ______________________
- One cost to cut or renegotiate: ______________________

### 4. Getting paid

- Invoices paid late this quarter: ______ of ______
- Average days late: ______
- Client(s) who are often late: ______________________
- One change for next quarter (deposit, shorter terms, reminders): ______________________

### 5. Tax pot check

- Tax pot balance: ______
- Best estimate of tax owed for the year so far (from your accountant, a calculator or last year's rate): ______
- Is the pot enough? yes / no
- Keep, raise or lower the set-aside percentage? ______ (see **tax-set-aside-planner.md**)

### 6. Looking ahead

- Lowest balance in the next 12 weeks (from **cash-flow-forecast.csv**): ______
- Big bills due next quarter: ______________________
- Income goal for next quarter: ______
- Three actions:
  1. ______________________
  2. ______________________
  3. ______________________

### 7. Housekeeping

- [ ] Bookkeeping folder backed up to a second location.
- [ ] Unclear rows marked for the accountant.
- [ ] This review saved in **ledger/quarterly-reviews/** as `YYYY-Qn-review.md`.

---

## Completed example

*The freelancer, clients and figures are made up for illustration.*

**Quarter:** 2026 Q1 (January-March)   **Done on:** 2 April

### 1. The numbers

| | This quarter | Last quarter | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Income | 6,850 | 5,400 | +1,450 |
| Expenses | 1,120 | 940 | +180 |
| Profit (income minus expenses) | 5,730 | 4,460 | +1,270 |
| Profit as % of income | 84% | 83% | +1 point |
| Owner pay taken | 3,000 | 3,000 | 0 |
| Tax pot balance at quarter end | 1,712.50 | 1,350 | |
| Money owed to me at quarter end | 1,500 | 650 | +850 |
| Business account balance at quarter end | 2,400 | 2,100 | +300 |

### 2. Where the money came from

| Client or income category | Income this quarter | % of total |
|---|---|---|
| Harbour Street Bakery (website design) | 3,600 | 53% |
| Willow Lane Yoga (logo design) | 1,600 | 23% |
| Northfield Accounting (consulting) | 1,650 | 24% |

- Largest single client's share of income: **53%**
- Step to reduce the risk: **send two proposals to new café and food clients this month, using the bakery case study.**

### 3. Where the money went

| Expense category | This quarter | Last quarter | Worth it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Software and subscriptions | 285 | 230 | review |
| Equipment | 79 | 0 | yes |
| Professional services | 135 | 135 | yes |
| Training and books | 89 | 0 | yes |
| Marketing | 38 | 120 | yes |
| Other categories combined | 494 | 455 | yes |

- Subscriptions no longer used: **a stock photo plan used twice in three months (19 a month).**
- Cost to cut: **cancel the stock plan and buy single images when needed.**

### 4. Getting paid

- Invoices paid late: **2 of 7**
- Average days late: **16**
- Often late: **Northfield Accounting**
- Change: **50% deposit before starting work for Northfield; payment terms reduced from 30 to 14 days for all new clients.**

### 5. Tax pot check

- Tax pot balance: **1,712.50** (25% of income)
- Best estimate of tax owed so far: **about 1,500** (based on last year's effective rate)
- Enough? **Yes, with a small margin.**
- Set-aside percentage: **keep at 25%** and recheck in Q2.

### 6. Looking ahead

- Lowest balance in next 12 weeks: **747.50 in late June, below the 1,500 buffer.**
- Big bills due: **insurance renewal (120) in April.**
- Income goal for Q2: **7,000.**
- Three actions:
  1. Chase the 1,500 owed by Willow Lane on its due date, 6 April.
  2. Send two new proposals to food businesses by 15 April.
  3. Delay the new monitor (350) until a June project is confirmed.

### 7. Housekeeping

- [x] Bookkeeping folder backed up.
- [x] Phone bill share marked for the accountant.
- [x] Saved as `2026-Q1-review.md`.
files.receipt-system.md:
# Receipt System

The goal: find any receipt or invoice in under ten seconds, years from now, without remembering anything. This system uses one folder structure and one naming rule. It works in any cloud drive or on your computer.

How long you must keep records depends on your country and business type (often several years). Check your local tax authority's guidance, and keep everything until you know.

---

## The folder structure

```
Bookkeeping/
  00 Inbox/
  2026/
    01 January/
      expenses/
      income/
      statements/
    02 February/
      expenses/
      income/
      statements/
    ...
  2027/
    ...
  ledger/
    income-expense-ledger.csv
    cash-flow-forecast.csv
    quarterly-reviews/
```

- **00 Inbox** is where everything goes the moment it arrives. You sort it during the monthly close.
- Each month has three folders: **expenses** (receipts and supplier invoices), **income** (invoices you sent) and **statements** (bank and card statements).
- Keep your ledger and forecast files in **ledger** so they never get lost among receipts.

Make a copy of the empty month folders at the start of each year.

## The naming rule

```
YYYY-MM-DD_category_what_amount.ext
```

Examples:

- `2026-03-07_equipment_hard-drive_79.00.pdf`
- `2026-03-15_travel_train-workshop_23.40.jpg`
- `2026-03-20_training_typography-course_89.00.pdf`

For invoices you send, use your invoice number first:

- `INV-031_harbour-street.pdf`

Why this works:

- Starting with the date makes files sort in time order automatically.
- The category and amount mean you can find a file by searching for "travel" or "79.00".
- No spaces avoids problems when files move between systems.
- The file name goes in the **invoice_or_receipt_ref** column of the ledger, so every row points to its proof.

## Getting receipts into the inbox

| Where the receipt comes from | What to do |
|---|---|
| Email receipt | Save as PDF straight into **00 Inbox**. Or forward it to a dedicated email folder and save weekly. |
| Paper receipt | Take a photo the same day with your phone, upload to **00 Inbox**. Make sure the date, supplier, items and total are readable. |
| Online account (software, hosting) | Many suppliers let you download invoices from their billing page. Download all last month's during the monthly close. |
| No receipt available | Write a short note file: date, supplier, amount, what it was, why it was for the business. Save it as `YYYY-MM-DD_category_what_amount_note.txt`. |

## Monthly routine (5 minutes, part of the monthly close)

1. Open **00 Inbox**.
2. Rename each file using the naming rule.
3. Move it into the right month and folder.
4. Copy the file name into the matching ledger row.
5. When the inbox is empty, you are done.

## Backups

- Keep your Bookkeeping folder in a cloud drive **and** make a copy on an external drive or second service at least once a quarter.
- Do the backup as part of your quarterly review so it never gets forgotten.

## Common problems

- **Faded paper receipts.** Thermal paper fades within months. Photograph every paper receipt on the day you get it.
- **Receipts in personal email.** Change the billing email on business subscriptions to your business address, so receipts arrive in one place.
- **One receipt for business and personal items.** Record only the business items in the ledger, and note "mixed receipt, personal items excluded" in the notes.
files.tax-set-aside-planner.md:
# Tax Set-Aside Planner

Most freelancers are not taxed automatically when a client pays them. The tax bill arrives later, sometimes many months later, and it can be large. The simplest protection is to move a fixed percentage of every payment into a separate account the day it arrives, and not touch it.

This planner helps you choose that percentage. It is a budgeting method, not tax advice: it does not tell you what you owe. Your actual tax depends on your country, your business structure, your total income, your allowable expenses and any other income you have. Use your local tax authority's guidance or an accountant to check your numbers, especially in your first year.

---

## Step 1: Find your best estimate of the effective rate

Your **effective rate** is your total tax and compulsory contributions for the year divided by your total income for the year. Use whichever of these you have, starting with the most reliable:

**Option A: You have a previous year's tax bill.**

```
Effective rate = total tax and contributions paid for last year
                 / total freelance income last year (before expenses)
```

**Option B: An accountant or official calculator has estimated it for you.** Use their figure.

**Option C: You have neither (first year).** Look up the official income tax and self-employed contribution rates for your country on your tax authority's website, estimate your profit for the year, and work out the total. If that is not possible yet, start with a cautious percentage and confirm it with a professional as soon as you can. Many freelancers start with somewhere around 25-30% to be on the safe side, but your right number may be lower or higher.

My effective rate estimate: ______ %   Source: ______________________

## Step 2: Add other things that come out of the same pot

Some freelancers also use the pot for sales tax or VAT collected from clients (if registered), or for advance payments that some countries require. If any apply to you, add them:

| Item | Percentage of income | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Income tax and contributions (from step 1) | ______ % | |
| Sales tax / VAT collected, if registered | ______ % | Often kept in its own pot instead |
| Other | ______ % | |
| **Subtotal** | ______ % | |

## Step 3: Add a buffer and round up

Add a safety buffer of a few percentage points, then round up to a whole number that is easy to calculate. A surplus at the end of the year is a pleasant surprise; a shortfall is a problem.

**My set-aside percentage: ______ %**

## Step 4: Make it automatic

- Open a separate savings account or pot named "Tax". Ideally one that takes a day or two to withdraw from.
- Every time a client payment lands, move your percentage across the same day and record a `transfer` row in the ledger.
- If your bank supports automatic rules, set one up. If not, do it during your weekly admin and check it in the monthly close.

## Step 5: Review every quarter

During **quarterly-review.md**, compare your tax pot balance with your best estimate of what you will owe for the year so far. Adjust the percentage if income has changed a lot or if your accountant gives you a new estimate.

## Worked example

*The person and numbers here are made up for illustration and do not reflect any real country's tax rules.*

Alex is a freelance illustrator in her second year.

**Step 1.** Last year Alex earned 38,000 in freelance income. Her tax bill and contributions for that year came to 8,740.

```
8,740 / 38,000 = 0.23, so 23%
```

**Step 2.** Alex is not registered for sales tax, and has no other items.

Subtotal: 23%

**Step 3.** Alex expects to earn more this year, which in her country may mean part of her income is taxed at a higher rate. She adds a 4-point buffer: 27%. She rounds up to **30%** because it is easy to work out in her head.

**Step 4.** A client pays her 1,500. She moves 450 (30%) into her tax pot the same afternoon and records:

```
2026-04-08,transfer,Tax set-aside,30% of INV-044 to tax pot,Own account,450.00,,business,Moved to tax-pot
```

**Step 5.** At the end of the first quarter, Alex has received 10,200 and her tax pot holds 3,060. Her accountant estimates her year's bill so far at about 2,500. She keeps 30% because her busiest months are still ahead, and plans to review again next quarter.

## Common questions

**What if I need the money in the tax pot?**
Treat it as not yours. If you are short, cut costs or chase invoices first. If you must borrow from the pot, write down the amount and repay it from the next payment, before anything else.

**What happens to any surplus?**
Once your bill for the year is paid, a surplus can become savings, an emergency fund or a bonus. Many freelancers like to keep the following year's advance payments, if their country has them, in the pot too.

**Should I set aside on the full payment or on profit?**
Setting aside on the full payment is simpler and more cautious. Tax is usually charged on profit (income minus allowable expenses), so the percentage from step 1 already reflects that if you calculated it against total income, as shown.
